introduction-more-than-just-a-phone-book.core: Route 53 is AWS's DNS service: an authoritative DNS with a 100% availability SLA, domain registration, health checking and traffic policies. Routing policies (simple, weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, multivalue, IP-based) turn DNS into a global traffic controller.

first_principles.problem: Teams treat DNS as a static address book and miss its role in failover and traffic shaping.
truths: Every connection starts with a DNS lookup.
DNS answers can vary by policy.

analogy.title: A smart switchboard rather than a phone book
analogy.story: It connects callers to the nearest open office, or the backup when one closes.
analogy.breaks: Switchboards connect in real time; DNS answers are cached for the TTL.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Users routed to nearest healthy region.

check.q: What availability SLA does Route 53 DNS offer?

routing-policies-simple-weighted-multi-v.core: Simple routing returns one record set (possibly multiple values, unhealth-checked). Weighted splits traffic across records by weight for canaries and blue/green. Multivalue answer returns up to eight healthy records at random, a simple form of client-side load balancing with health checks.

first_principles.problem: A team wants to send 5% of traffic to a new stack without a load balancer change.
truths: DNS can return different answers to different resolvers.

analogy.title: Handing out directions at a fork in the road
analogy.story: Always the same way (simple), 95 of 100 people left and 5 right (weighted), or any of several open roads (multivalue).
analogy.breaks: Directions are followed immediately; DNS caching makes splits approximate.

check.q: How many healthy records can a multivalue answer return?

routing-policies-latency-vs-geolocation.core: Latency-based routing answers with the AWS region that gives the user's resolver the lowest measured network latency, optimising performance. Geolocation routing answers based on the user's location (continent, country, US state) for compliance, localisation or licensing, with a default record for unmatched locations.

first_principles.problem: EU users must be served from EU regions for data residency, but other users should get the fastest region.
truths: Resolver location approximates user location (EDNS Client Subnet helps).

analogy.title: Choosing a supermarket by drive time versus by country rules
analogy.story: Usually go to the quickest; but some products must be bought in your own country.
analogy.breaks: Drivers know where they are; DNS infers location from resolver IPs.

example.title: Residency + performance
flow: Geolocation: Europe → EU alias record set
EU set: latency between eu-west-1 and eu-central-1
example.outcome: routing by both law and speed.

check.q: Why add a default geolocation record?
check.a: Requests from locations with no matching record would otherwise get no answer (NXDOMAIN/NODATA).

geoproximity-routing-shifting-traffic-by.core: Geoproximity routing sends users to the geographically nearest resource (AWS region or lat/long coordinates), with a bias (−99 to +99) that expands or shrinks each resource's catchment area. It's configured via Traffic Flow and lets you gradually shift traffic between regions geographically.

first_principles.problem: A new region should gradually take more nearby traffic from an overloaded one.

analogy.title: Moving school catchment boundaries
analogy.story: Expand one school's zone so more nearby families attend it.
analogy.breaks: School zones change yearly; bias changes take effect after DNS TTLs.

example.title: Shifting to a new region
flow: More of Eastern Europe routed there

check.q: What does a positive bias do in geoproximity routing?
check.a: Expands the resource's geographic area so it attracts more traffic.

failover-routing-active-passive-disaster.core: Failover routing answers with the primary record while its health check passes and switches to the secondary when it fails. It's the DNS backbone of active-passive DR: primary region (or ALB) and a standby region or static S3 maintenance page, with low TTLs and evaluate-target-health on alias records.

first_principles.problem: During a regional outage, someone must manually change DNS, which takes time and depends on the control plane.
truths: Health checks run continuously in the data plane.
Caching delays the switch by the TTL.

analogy.title: An automatic transfer switch for a building's power
analogy.story: When mains fails, it switches to the generator by itself.
analogy.breaks: Transfer switches act in milliseconds; DNS clients may cache old answers for the TTL.

example.title: Active-passive web app
flow: Primary: alias → us-east-1 ALB, health check on /health
example.outcome: automated DR at the DNS layer.

check.q: What determines when failover routing switches to the secondary?
check.a: The primary record's health check (or alias target health) becoming unhealthy.

health-checks-the-heartbeat-monitor.core: Route 53 health checks probe endpoints (HTTP/HTTPS/TCP, optional string matching) from checkers in multiple regions, mark them unhealthy when enough checkers fail, and can be calculated (combining child checks) or based on CloudWatch alarms for private resources. They drive DNS answers and can trigger alerts.

first_principles.problem: A private database endpoint can't be health-checked from the internet, and one flaky checker shouldn't trigger failover.
derivation: **Endpoint checks** with path and string match.

analogy.title: Several doctors independently checking a pulse
analogy.story: You only declare an emergency if most agree.
analogy.breaks: Doctors examine the patient; checkers only see what the endpoint returns, so design meaningful /health pages.

example.title: Calculated health check
flow: Region marked down only on broad failure

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No failover on one bad instance.

check.q: How can Route 53 health-check a private resource?
check.a: With a health check based on a CloudWatch alarm that monitors the resource.

alias-records-vs-cname-records.core: A CNAME maps a name to another name and can't exist at the zone apex (example.com). A Route 53 alias record points directly to AWS resources (CloudFront, ALB/NLB, S3 website, API Gateway, another record in the zone), works at the apex, resolves inside Route 53 with no extra lookup, follows target IP changes automatically and is free for AWS targets.

first_principles.problem: example.com must point to a CloudFront distribution, but DNS forbids a CNAME at the apex.
truths: DNS forbids CNAMEs at the apex alongside SOA/NS.
derivation: Use **CNAME** only for non-AWS names on subdomains.
Remember alias **queries are free** for AWS targets.

analogy.title: A forwarding address versus a direct address the post office updates itself
analogy.story: The forwarding address sends mail elsewhere; the alias delivers straight to wherever the resource is now.
analogy.breaks: Post offices are slow to update; alias records reflect target changes immediately.

check.q: Why can't you use a CNAME at example.com?
check.a: DNS rules forbid a CNAME at the zone apex because it must coexist with SOA and NS records.
